all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: usability
concepts.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

defining_facts.text: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: efficiency
concepts.definition: Efficiency is one of the measures of usability that shows how fast a user can do what they want to do.

defining_facts.text: The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: degree of freedom
concepts.definition: Degree of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space; in 3D space, an object can have six degrees of freedom: three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes, and three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch.

defining_facts.text: The concept of degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space.

In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.
In a virtual world, motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

concepts.name: empirical study
concepts.definition: Empirical study is a usability-testing stage in interactive system development, performed after code testing, that systematically tests a fully implemented system with end users through a controlled experiment to collect and analyze data for assessing overall usability.

defining_facts.text: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.
The empirical study stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development and is typically not part of other software development in which end users are not involved.
In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.

The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, usability study, or empirical research, is a stage in interactive system development in which the usability of a developed system is evaluated with end users.
In interactive system development, empirical evaluation follows the code testing stage, which produces an executable system but does not establish that the system is usable.

A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

A controlled experiment used for usability evaluation is generally referred to as empirical research, an empirical study, or a user study, and in the context of usability evaluation it can also be called a usability study.

An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects.

An empirical study, after a system has been fully implemented, is the process of setting up an experiment, executing the experiment, and collecting empirical data for analysis to measure the usability of the implemented interface.

The first stage in an empirical study is formulating a research question, and the experiment is conducted to find the answer to that question, with observations or empirical data collection and data analysis performed based on the question.
Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, empirical research, or usability research, means observation in the real world of real users.
Empirical evaluation is carried out at the end, when the system is fully implemented, to obtain an idea of the overall usability of the system.
The empirical research process has four stages, the first stage being research question framing and the second stage being variables.

In empirical research, research question framing addresses broader generalizable questions that are untestable by framing multiple testable research questions, collecting objective data for each, reaching a definite conclusion for each, and combining those conclusions to draw a conclusion about the untestable questions.

In the variables stage of empirical research, the variables in the testable questions are identified to design an experiment; the two most important variable types are independent variables, or factors, which can take levels or values, and dependent variables, which depend on the factors and levels.

concepts.name: user group
concepts.definition: A user group is a category of potential users for which a virtual tour's content and features are tailored.

defining_facts.text: Before the actual virtual tour experience begins, the user chooses a user group, indicated by icons for the user categories pilgrims, students, or tourists.

concepts.name: experiment
concepts.definition: An experiment is the designed and executed part of an empirical study that collects and compares objective data to answer a research question and measure the usability of an implemented interface.

defining_facts.text: An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.

concepts.name: independent variable
concepts.definition: An independent variable is a variable whose values are assigned and controlled; these values are called levels and are used to design an experiment.

defining_facts.text: A variable whose values are assigned and controlled is called an independent variable, also called a factor.
The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called the levels of that independent variable or factor.

Factors combined with their levels give the test conditions for an experiment and are used to design the experiment; in the text-entry example, the interface factor has two levels, the course's design and MS Word, and these two levels give two test conditions in which text entry speed is observed with each.

A dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on an independent variable or factor, specifically on its levels; in research question 3 (RQ3), the text entry rate (TER) is the dependent variable because its value depends on the interface, specifically the interface levels.

In the variables stage of empirical research, the variables in the testable questions are identified to design an experiment; the two most important variable types are independent variables, or factors, which can take levels or values, and dependent variables, which depend on the factors and levels.

concepts.name: level
concepts.definition: A level is a value assigned to an independent variable or factor in an experiment.

defining_facts.text: The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called the levels of that independent variable or factor.

Factors combined with their levels give the test conditions for an experiment and are used to design the experiment; in the text-entry example, the interface factor has two levels, the course's design and MS Word, and these two levels give two test conditions in which text entry speed is observed with each.

A dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on an independent variable or factor, specifically on its levels; in research question 3 (RQ3), the text entry rate (TER) is the dependent variable because its value depends on the interface, specifically the interface levels.

concepts.name: test condition
concepts.definition: A test condition is a combination of factor levels that is used to design an experiment.

defining_facts.text: Factors combined with their levels give the test conditions for an experiment and are used to design the experiment; in the text-entry example, the interface factor has two levels, the course's design and MS Word, and these two levels give two test conditions in which text entry speed is observed with each.

never_defined.name: user characteristic
never_defined.definition: User characteristic is an attribute of a user, such as needs, expectations, skills, or typing behavior, that designers consider when designing systems to match users' needs and expectations.

never_defined.name: interface
never_defined.definition: An interface is the way a system interfaces with users, its environment, and other systems, letting users provide input, see outcomes, and act on outcomes; on a computer screen it is the whole content seen there.

never_defined.name: task
never_defined.definition: A task is an activity that users perform, involving a sequence of user actions and corresponding interface changes, and whose performance data can be used to evaluate an interface.

never_defined.name: participant
never_defined.definition: A participant is a user selected for an experiment on the basis of a user profile so that the selected users form a representative sample of the whole user group.

never_defined.name: empirical data
never_defined.definition: Empirical data is data collected in an experiment or empirical study that answers a research question, and it is processed and tested for statistical significance before conclusions are drawn.

never_defined.name: text input interface
never_defined.definition: A text input interface is an interface that lets a user enter text.

never_defined.name: text entry speed
never_defined.definition: Text entry speed is objective data that is logged as characters per minute (CPM) and used to determine which text entry interface is faster.

never_defined.name: objective data
never_defined.definition: Objective data is data, such as text entry speed or task performance data, that can be collected and analyzed to draw objective conclusions independently of users' subjective interpretation.

never_defined.name: experiment design
never_defined.definition: Experiment design is used to select a representative sample of potential users as participants, using a well-defined user profile.

never_defined.name: sample
never_defined.definition: Sample is a subset of all potential users chosen for an experiment or empirical study to represent the larger population, so conclusions about that population are valid.

never_defined.name: age group
never_defined.definition: An age group is one of the similarities that members of a homogeneous user group can share.

never_defined.name: educational background
never_defined.definition: Educational background is one of the backgrounds that can be similar among members of a homogeneous user group.

never_defined.name: socio-economic background
never_defined.definition: Socio-economic background is one of the backgrounds that may be similar among members of a homogeneous user group.

never_defined.name: cultural background
never_defined.definition: Cultural background is one of the similarities that members of a homogeneous user group may share, along with age, educational, or socio-economic background.

never_defined.name: homogeneous subset
never_defined.definition: A homogeneous subset is a user group whose members have the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds.

never_defined.name: heterogeneous user group
never_defined.definition: A heterogeneous user group is a user group for which using a homogeneous subset is not reliable for drawing conclusions.

never_defined.name: user profile characteristic
never_defined.definition: A user profile characteristic is one of the well-defined elements of a user profile that, in experiment design, defines a user and is the only basis for selecting experiment participants.

never_defined.name: typing behavior
never_defined.definition: Typing behavior is a user characteristic that can vary with age and computer-use frequency, and it is considered when choosing experiment participants based on user profiles.

never_defined.name: typing speed
never_defined.definition: Typing speed is a user characteristic that can differ among users and must be considered when choosing experiment participants based on user profiles.

never_defined.name: number of participants
never_defined.definition: Number of participants is the count of participants in a controlled empirical experiment, generally assumed to be between 12 and 25 to draw reliable conclusions.

never_defined.name: task performance data
never_defined.definition: Task performance data are mostly objective data collected from users performing tasks in a controlled experiment evaluating an interface, and are analyzed to draw conclusions about the interface.

never_defined.name: typing task
never_defined.definition: A typing task is a task used to compare typing interfaces.

never_defined.name: typing interface
never_defined.definition: A typing interface is an interface compared using typing tasks.

never_defined.name: random piece of text
never_defined.definition: A random piece of text is a text used for a typing task to compare typing interfaces, but it is not a representative task.

never_defined.name: text string
never_defined.definition: A text string is a piece of text that can be used as a representative task in a typing task for comparing typing interfaces when chosen by certain metrics and measures.

never_defined.name: metric
never_defined.definition: A Metric is used, along with measures, to choose representative typing tasks for comparing typing interfaces.

never_defined.name: measure
never_defined.definition: Measure is used, along with metrics, to choose representative text strings for typing tasks that compare typing interfaces.

never_defined.name: typing skill
never_defined.definition: Typing skill is a user skill indirectly encompassed by representative tasks used to compare typing interfaces.

never_defined.name: experimental study
never_defined.definition: An experimental study is a study in which tasks can be assigned using either a within-subject or a between-subjects design.

never_defined.name: confounding variable
never_defined.definition: A confounding variable is, for example, a practice effect in a within-subject design that confounds the analysis by adding noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than to the interface.

never_defined.name: task sequence
never_defined.definition: Task sequence is the sequence of tasks allocated to a participant, which can be randomized or systematically varied to reduce the practice effect in a within-subject design.

never_defined.name: system implementation process
never_defined.definition: The system implementation process is a process that includes its fourth stage, data analysis, in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about a design's efficacy.

never_defined.name: statistical significance
never_defined.definition: Statistical significance is a reported result of a statistical significance test of empirical data from an experiment, used before drawing conclusions about whether a difference, such as in group means, is statistically significant.

never_defined.name: population
never_defined.definition: Population is, in empirical interface studies, the larger actual population, such as any user and any text-entry interface, rather than the sample of users from which data are obtained, and the conclusions of interest are about it.

never_defined.name: observed data difference
never_defined.definition: An Observed data difference is a difference in observed data that a statistical significance test indicates is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions.

never_defined.name: mean text-entry speed
never_defined.definition: Mean text-entry speed is the value for each group used when comparing two text-entry interfaces.

never_defined.name: relative difference
never_defined.definition: Relative difference is used when comparing two text-entry interfaces to consider the difference between the groups' mean text-entry speeds rather than their absolute values.

never_defined.name: absolute value
never_defined.definition: Absolute value is a value that may be contrasted with the relative difference between mean text-entry speeds when comparing two text-entry interfaces.

never_defined.name: experimental design
never_defined.definition: Experimental design is one of the things on which the method for performing a statistical significance test depends, along with the nature of the input data.

never_defined.name: absolute difference
never_defined.definition: Absolute difference is a difference in group means that can be included in the result of a statistical significance test.

never_defined.name: group mean
never_defined.definition: Group mean is a mean whose absolute difference can be included in the result of a statistical significance test.

never_defined.name: t value
never_defined.definition: T value is a value that can be included in the result of a statistical significance test.

never_defined.name: paired sample t-test
never_defined.definition: Paired sample t-test is a parametric statistical significance test used for a within-subject design with one factor and two levels to show whether differences between the levels are statistically significant.

never_defined.name: parametric test
never_defined.definition: A parametric test is a statistical significance test that belongs to one of two groups of such tests.

never_defined.name: non-parametric test
never_defined.definition: A non-parametric test is a statistical significance test that can be used in between-subject or within-subject experimental designs with one or more factors having two or more levels.

never_defined.name: scale of measurement
never_defined.definition: A scale of measurement is a scale in an experimental design, such as a nominal or categorical scale.

never_defined.name: nominal scale
never_defined.definition: A nominal scale is a scale of measurement in an experimental design.

never_defined.name: chi-square test
never_defined.definition: Chi-square test is a non-parametric test used for a between-subject experimental design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels.

never_defined.name: McNemar's test
never_defined.definition: McNemar's test is a non-parametric test that is used for a within-subject design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels.

never_defined.name: independent samples t-test
never_defined.definition: An Independent samples t-test is a parametric test that can be used in a between-subject design with one factor having two levels and no other condition mentioned.

never_defined.name: Mann-Whitney U test
never_defined.definition: The Mann-Whitney U test is a non-parametric test that can be used for a between-subject design with one factor having two levels.

never_defined.name: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
never_defined.definition: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a non-parametric statistical significance test that can be used in a within-subject design with one factor having two levels.

never_defined.name: analysis of variance
never_defined.definition: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is a parametric test that is used for between-subject or within-subject designs with one factor having more than two levels, or with two or more factors each having two or more levels.

never_defined.name: one-way analysis of variance
never_defined.definition: One-way analysis of variance is a parametric test used in between-subject designs for one factor with more than two levels.

never_defined.name: factorial analysis of variance
never_defined.definition: Factorial analysis of variance is a parametric test used for between-subject designs with two or more factors, each having two or more levels.

never_defined.name: Kruskal-Wallis test
never_defined.definition: The Kruskal-Wallis test is a test that can be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels.

never_defined.name: repeated measures analysis of variance
never_defined.definition: Repeated measures analysis of variance is a parametric test that can be used for a within-subject design with one factor having three or more levels, or with two or more factors each having two or more levels.

never_defined.name: Friedman test
never_defined.definition: Friedman test is a non-parametric test that can be used for a within-subject design with one factor having three or more levels, or for a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels.
